body.text: Soon after reports of the Democratic Party’s sweep in mid-term elections to the United States Congress and Senate emerged, the Indian media was flooded with reports of why this is good news for New Delhi.

The Indian Express reported that the result evoked a “collective sigh of relief in Delhi” in hopes that it would “bring back the checks and balances in the American establishment.” Another report suggested that a growing number of Indian American legislators, at six following the mid-term elections, will allow them to translate their electoral success into meaningful influence over policy, especially those concerning India-U.S. relations.

The mood in India’s foreign ministry is reportedly “cautiously optimistic.” According to a report in the Business Standard, Indian officials hope that the change would give India more “manoeuvring space,” especially on issues of “immigration, trade and energy.”

U.S. President Donald Trump’s immigration policies have adversely affected the Indian American community, which comprises the second largest Asian origin population living in the U.S. His suspension of the Program Electronic Review Management (PERM) applications for major technology and IT firms, including Microsoft, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, and HCL, has frozen employment-based green card pathways for H-1B holders.
Given the Democratic Party’s traditionally pro-legal immigration position, their victory is definitely good news for Indian immigrants to the U.S.
However, what is good for Indian Americans does not necessarily translate to good for the current government of India.

Unlike Trump, who ignored the Narendra Modi government’s imperfect democratic record, many Democrats – including Indian American members – have been vocal in expressing their concerns over the erosion of democracy in India. Pramila Jayapal, who won her sixth U.S. congressional term in the recent mid-term elections, has openly criticized the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls in India. In a post on X, she expressed concerns about the “actions of the Indian government to purge 130 million people from the voting rolls,” comparing it with the Trump administration’s moves to “undermine voting rights” in the U.S.

Notably, she was also among the six Democratic Party lawmakers who sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on October 16 urging him to raise concerns over democratic freedoms with Indian officials during his India visit.

Some have argued that the Democratic victories will increase legislative oversight over Trump’s unilateral policymaking and that this will positively impact bilateral ties. However, there are certain structural limits. While the Democratic Party can pass bills that seek to repeal tariffs imposed on partner countries, Trump can still use his veto power to overturn legislation. Overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate i.e., 290 votes in the House and 67 in the Senate, with all members voting, which the Democrats are unlikely to reach.

Before results were announced, Trump had publicly warned he would become “Mr. Veto” if Democrats took control of Congress. He reaffirmed this soon after election results indicated a strong showing by the Democrats by posting an image of a red cap bearing the word “VETO” on Truth Social, signaling his readiness to leverage his constitutional powers to advance his personal agenda.
The Trump administration’s recent waiver of Russia sanctions and the diesel deal are likely to be the top priority for scrutiny by the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress.

Given the strong bipartisan support for Ukraine in the past, including from many of Trump’s Republicans, it is possible that Congress will be able to muster the supermajority needed to override the presidential veto on legislation concerning action against Moscow, and in support of Kyiv. In such a scenario, New Delhi has a lot to lose as it would make Indian purchases of discounted Russian oil more expensive and difficult. As a Quad partner, India could come under pressure to call out Moscow’s actions in Ukraine.

While the Democrats’ victory brought in much-needed relief for Indian equities, with shares logging their biggest gains in seven months on hopes that it would bring an end to the U.S.-Iran war, questions remain over whether the immediate relief is merely temporary.

On Iran, there is much speculation on what Trump’s next move might be. Reports suggest that he has already made preparations for a new military campaign against Iran that could involve strikes on nuclear facilities and civilian infrastructure. As a lame duck president facing a potentially hostile legislature, Trump is likely to lean into foreign policy, where executive authority is substantially stronger. Just days after claiming that the U.S. did not have “immediate plans to strike Iran,” Trump hinted at potential strikes when asked about his plans regarding resumption of military action in Iran, leaving hopes of a diplomatic resolution a distant dream.

Amidst this uncertainty, not all hope is lost for the India-U.S. partnership. New Delhi’s deep bipartisan ties, which extend well beyond the White House, have allowed it to smoothly navigate across two decades of different administrations. Having direct relationships with influential lawmakers – such as New York Democrat Gregory Meeks, likely the next House Foreign Affairs Committee chair – gives India vital leverage during the upcoming transition.

Yet, assuming that Trump’s defeat at the midterm elections automatically implies an improvement in U.S.-India relations oversimplifies a complex dynamic. For now, shelving the pending trade deal and taking a wait-and-watch approach through the transition is New Delhi’s safest bet.
